java.text: public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
java.explain: The task: find two distinct positions whose values add to the target; exactly one pair exists.
Start with an empty map of earlier values so only already seen indices can complete a pair and reuse is impossible.
Move left to right focusing on one position at a time so every value gets a fair chance as the later partner.
Compute the partner needed (target minus current) and look only in the earlier map, since storing first would reuse the same index.
Test if the needed partner is already mapped, missing means no earlier pair exists and checking before storing protects distinctness.
Return the earlier mapped index with the current one; safe only because the check ran before the store, so positions differ.
End of the partner test: a miss falls through to store the current value for later positions.
Save the current value with its index for future partners, adding only after the check so the same position cannot match itself.
End of one pass iteration: the stored value is now visible to every later position.
Report no pair when the full pass finds nothing, which confirms no pair of distinct positions completes the target.

practice.intent: Same pattern, different numbers so you reproduce the reasoning.
practice.title: Two Sum — fresh numbers (pair-sum drill)
practice.statement: Same pattern, new numbers. You are given an array nums of distinct integers and an integer target; return the indices [i, j], with i < j, of the two values that add up to target. Exactly one such pair exists in every test.
hints: The partner each value needs is target minus that value.
Record the index of every value you have already walked past, then look each partner up directly.

practice.intent: Same pattern with the edge case the original hides.
practice.title: Two Sum — edge cases (pair-sum drill)
practice.statement: This time the numbers can be negative or zero and the matching pair may sit anywhere in the array. Given nums of 3 to 7 distinct integers and a target, return the indices [i, j], i < j, of the unique two values whose sum equals target. Exactly one pair exists in every test.
hints: Nothing in the lookup idea assumes positive values.
Negative targets work the same way — the complement you look up may itself be negative.

practice.intent: Same signature, different question: the twist tests whether the idea transfers.
practice.title: Two Sum — twist: values (pair-sum drill)
practice.statement: Given nums of distinct integers and a target, return the two values themselves that add up to target, ordered smaller first as [a, b]. Do not return indices. Exactly one such pair exists in every test.
hints: Find the pair exactly as before, then swap the indices for the values behind them.
The two returned values must be ordered, so compare them once before returning.

practice.intent: Same pattern, different numbers so you reproduce the reasoning.
practice.title: Number of Islands — fresh grids (island-count drill)
practice.statement: You are given a rectangular binary grid where 1 marks land and 0 marks water. An island is a group of 1s connected horizontally or vertically, and the grid edges are surrounded by water. Count how many islands the grid holds. Test grids are small, at most 5 rows by 6 columns.
hints: Walk every cell once and flood-fill each unvisited land cell you meet.
Mark visited land as you flood so each island is counted exactly once.

practice.intent: Same pattern with the edge case the original hides.
practice.title: Number of Islands — edge cases (island-count drill)
practice.statement: Same island count with the boundary grids. The grid may be a single cell, all land, or all water. A 1x1 grid holding 1 is one island, a 1x1 grid holding 0 is none, and a solid 2x2 block of land is a single island.
hints: A single cell is the smallest grid the task allows.
All-land and all-water grids test whether both extremes behave.

practice.intent: Same signature, different question: the twist tests whether the idea transfers.
practice.title: Number of Islands — twist: water regions (island-count drill)
practice.statement: Twist: count regions of water instead of land. A water region is a group of 0s connected horizontally or vertically, and the ocean touching the grid edges counts like any other region. Return how many such regions the grid holds.
hints: Run the same flood-fill idea with the roles swapped: spread through 0s.
Corner-touching water still connects only through shared edges, not diagonals.
